transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-11-05
Start time: 15:00 PST (US-Pac)
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Alex Carter (Redwood AE), Priya Desai (Redwood SE), Maya Thompson (Aperture Head of ML), Jordan Reyes (Infra), Ethan Park (CTO)

Auto-generated Summary (may be imperfect):
A discovery call focused on cost/unit economics for an LLM-powered search/QA product. Customer is evaluating Redwood Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private. Key concerns: per-token costs, how batching and KV/prefix caching reduce unit cost, latency SLOs for 95th perc, budget cap (target $10k / month initially), and security/compliance questions for private deployment. Next steps: pricing sheet, benchmark plan, share traffic sample, schedule POC.

Topics: pricing, batching, KV cache, quantization, dedicated commitments, pilot/benchmarks, security/questions (SAML, KMS)

Transcript:
[00:00] Alex: hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh we'll do a quick intros then jump into your goals for this evaluation. I'm alex carter from Redwood, AE on the account.
[00:18] Maya: yeah hi I'm maya, head of ML at aperture insights, and we have jordan infra and ethan our cto. thanks for the time.
[00:28] Priya: hi all, priya desai, solutions engineer, i'll focus on performance and cost details today.
[00:36] Ethan: good to meet you. quick context - we're building a search/qa assistant for enterprise docs, first phase ~100k monthly active users, typical prompt length 60-120 tokens, and we want sub-300ms p50 latency on queries but can tolerate p95 up to 1.2s, budget for pilot ~ $8k- $12k/mo.
[01:05] Jordan: infra constraint - data residency in us-east, and must support SAML SSO and audit logs. potentially consider private deployment if contractually required.
[01:22] Alex: got it. so main axis we'll look at is hosted for speed to market, dedicated for predictable throughput/cost, and private for strict controls. maya, can you share what you mean by budget - is that per team or global?
[01:38] Maya: initial budget is global for the first phase, about 10k a month. We're running experiments; if it scales well we'll expand. important for us is unit economics - cost per query.
[01:48] Priya: yeah, so i'll break down per-token math and levers - batching, KV/prefix cache, and quantization. baseline: our hosted per-token list price for the curated open models ranges by model family; for a moderate LLM used for search we usually model X tokens in/ out per request so your per-query cost depends on prompt + completion tokens.
[02:15] Maya: can you give an example? like per-query numbers for say 180 tokens total?
[02:20] Priya: sure. rough example: on hosted, with our mid-sized open model, list price is approximately $0.0008 per 1k input tokens and $0.0016 per 1k output tokens - rough numbers - so 180 tokens (~120 in, 60 out) is about 0.00096 + 0.000096? sorry, math slip - let me restate: 180 tokens is 0.18 of a 1k unit, so you'd be roughly $0.00014 to $0.0003 per request depending on in/out split. those numbers are small per request but scale quickly.
[03:02] Jordan: ok but what about batching? our traffic is bursty - bursts of 200 qps for short windows. does batching help reduce cost? and does it increase latency?
[03:14] Priya: yes. batching groups simultaneous requests to amortize GPU compute and reduces per-token cost - essentially better throughput. There's a tradeoff: you can configure max wait time (say 5-20ms) and max batch size. For interactive search, we tune for small max wait (~10ms) to keep p50 low while still achieving some batching. For very bursty traffic you can get 15-30% cost reduction with continuous batching. Also KV/prefix caching is big for search: if many requests share the same prefix or document context, you cache keys in memory (we call it KV cache) and avoid re-computing earlier layers - that can yield 40-70% token compute savings on repeated contexts.
[03:58] Maya: is KV cache available on hosted? and does it require session stickiness?
[04:05] Priya: hosted supports prefix and KV caching for sessiony workloads; we give an API to set cache keys. For predictable SLOs we recommend dedicated where you control eviction and memory sizes. Hosted has managed cache but dedicated gives you more predictable hit rates.
[04:25] Ethan: curious about quantization - you mentioned quantization-friendly profiles earlier? how much does that affect cost and latency?
[04:32] Priya: quantized models (int8, int4) run faster and use less memory which reduces cost per token. For many open models we see 20-40% cost reduction with int8 without significant quality loss; int4 can go further but depends on model. Redwood Optimize gives model+quantization recommendations per workload, we can propose candidate models that balance quality vs cost.
[04:58] Jordan: for dedicated, what's the pricing model? is it a flat monthly capacity cost or also per token?
[05:05] Alex: dedicated is a reserved capacity contract - you pay for the pool (monthly commit) which gives predictable throughput. Some add-ons charge per-token for storage or long-term archival, but generally it's capacity-based. We can model your expected tokens per month to show equivalent cost vs hosted. For pilots, we often do a short benchmark on hosted and a projected dedicated TCO.
[05:30] Maya: can you show a sample TCO? like if we do 10M tokens per month what's the difference?
[05:36] Priya: high level: hosted might be simpler: multiply per-token price by 10M; dedicated will amortize GPU hours across that traffic and often comes in lower per-token once you hit steady high utilization. ballpark example: hosted could be $X per 1M tokens ~ (we'll send exact numbers) leading to say $Y for 10M, dedicated with a small pool might be 20-40% cheaper depending on batch utilization and cache hit rate. we'll run the numbers and share a TCO.
[06:10] Ethan: we will likely want a pilot that runs both hosted and dedicated benchmarks to get real numbers - especially since our average prompt length and cache hit rates matter.
[06:20] Alex: totally. the benchmark POC is our typical next step. priya, we'll need a test plan.
[06:25] Priya: yes, i'll propose a 2-4 hour controlled benchmark that simulates your traffic, measuring p50/p95 latency, throughput, and per-token cost under different batch and cache settings. we'll include a hosted run and a dedicated run (small reserved pool).
[06:41] Jordan: what about private - is that more expensive? we have compliance requirements that might force private deployment.
[06:47] Alex: private (VPC/on-prem) has a platform fee + support and then infra costs. It's typically higher upfront due to licensing/support and customer infra. But for very large and regulated workloads it's worth it. We can produce a private pricing estimate if you need it.
[06:59] Maya: security questions - do you support KMS integration, SAML SSO, audit logs? we need evidence for SOC2.
[07:07] Priya: yes - hosted supports enterprise features like SAML and audit logs for enterprise tiers; dedicated and private give you KMS/HSM integrations and a richer audit trail. we'll share our security pack (SOC2 report, whitepaper).
[07:20] Ethan: latency SLAs? do you have SLOs for p95 on hosted?
[07:25] Alex: hosted has published latency profiles, but dedicated comes with SLA-backed targets for throughput and latency depending on pool size. For strict p95 targets we recommend dedicated or private.
[07:36] Maya: i want to understand operational levers - if we tune batch size aggressively, can we push costs down 50%? or is that unrealistic?
[07:44] Priya: 50% is optimistic unless you have very high cache hit rates and high concurrency. Typical savings combine: batching 15-30%, KV cache 40-60% (if your workload repeats context), and quantization 20-40%. Combined you might see large reductions but it depends on overlap - they multiply not simply add. We'll model with your sample traffic.
[08:12] Jordan: question on sticky sessions - does caching require sticky routing to a GPU instance?
[08:18] Priya: you can do sticky routing for session affinity but we also support global distributed KV caches and replication for hit consistency. on dedicated you get more control over eviction policy.
[08:30] Maya: how do you measure token counts though? our accounting wants to map to business metrics - tokens per user session, etc.
[08:36] Alex: console exposes token-level breakdowns per route and per model; we can show token histograms and cost by route so you can link to product metrics.
[08:46] Ethan: for the pilot, we want an acceptance criteria: p95 < 1.2s, cost per 1k tokens <= a threshold we define, and accuracy/regression checks on a small eval set. can you include that?
[08:58] Priya: yes we'll include those in the POC plan.
[09:02] Maya: what about burst pricing - if we spike beyond the reserved capacity?
[09:07] Alex: for dedicated we offer configurable autoscale bursts and fallbacks to hosted or lower-cost model variants. There's a cost tradeoff: bursts billed at a different rate or require a buffer. We'll show options in the pricing sheet.
[09:20] Jordan: do you support multi-model routing? e.g., route high-value queries to a larger model and cheaper model for low-value queries?
[09:26] Priya: yes - smart routing by policy. you can route by latency or cost tier, and Redwood will fallback to compatible variants. That helps control unit economics while preserving quality on critical queries.
[09:38] Maya: any gotchas running benchmarks? what should we measure?
[09:42] Priya: measure throughput, latency percentiles, tokens consumed, cache hit rate, and model quality on your eval prompts. Also simulate realistic concurrency and cold-starts for KV cache. We'll include a recommended script.
[09:58] Ethan: ok sounds good. we want to see end-to-end numbers not just synthetic.
[10:02] Alex: understood. we'll follow up with the pricing/TCO and bench plan. any other questions?
[10:08] Maya: one more - can you share approximate lead time for dedicated pool setup?
[10:13] Priya: typically 2-4 weeks depending on capacity and region; shorter if you accept existing shared infra for pilot. Private can be longer due to customer infra setup.
[10:24] Jordan: thanks. we'll share sample traffic and top prompts.
[10:27] Alex: perfect. recap: Alex sends pricing/TCO, Priya sends POC plan and batching recommendations, maya shares traffic, and we'll schedule benchmark week of 11/15.
[10:39] Maya: thanks, bye.
[10:41] Alex: thanks everyone, bye.

End of transcript.
